sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An upper-low will continue to remain offshore bringing light lowland rain and mountain snow to the area today. More active weather arrives through the week as a series of systems brings widespread precipitation, gusty winds, high surf, and the increasing potential for coastal flooding.

sections.title: Short term (today through Tuesday)
paragraphs: An upper level low remains parked offshore western Washington this morning, which will continue to spin up showers into the area throughout the remainder of the day. Latest radar imagery shows showers continuously moving onshore, with some showers, especially over the coast could see a slight convective activity with them in the afternoon. Otherwise, most locations can expect on and off showers this afternoon. High temperatures generally in the mid to upper 40s for most interior locations. Additionally, a Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect for the Pacific Coast for the high tide this morning.

Upper level troughing will become more prominent into Monday, with a wave of steadier precipitation entering the region. Most of the QPF will be located in the Olympics and the Cascades, with showers over the interior. Additionally, snow levels will start off generally around 2000 to 3000 feet late tonight into early Monday morning, rising to 4000 feet by Monday afternoon. A Winter Weather Advisory remains in effect for the Olympics through Monday afternoon, where Hurricane Ridge could see around 5 to 10 inches of snow. Showers will continue throughout Monday with another front arriving to the area by Tuesday.

A stronger front will move over western Washington on Tuesday into Wednesday as the aforementioned upper level low deepens along the coast. Expect widespread lowland rain, along with mountain snow as snow levels in the Cascades will be generally around 3000 to 3500 feet. We'll also see locally breezy winds across the area, more notably along the coast. This system will also likely bring another round of high surf to the coast. Additionally, high astronomical tides combined with the weather impacts from these systems, will increase the threat for coastal flooding, most notably along the Pacific Coast during high surf on Tuesday.

sections.title: Long term (Tuesday night through Saturday)
paragraphs: Latest ensembles continue to highlight additional stronger systems entering the area Wednesday into Thursday, with another round of widespread rain, breezy winds, and mountain snow. Rainfall will likely be heaviest Wednesday night into Thursday, especially over the Olympics, where the Skokomish River may have to be monitored as rainfall drives it above flood stage. Additionally, confidence is increasing for the potential of moderate to major coastal flooding stages being reached along portions of the Grays Harbor County coastline during Wednesday tides, and high surf may only enhance these impacts. The tides increase more significantly for the Strait and Puget Sound coastlines later in the week around Tuesday onward, and the potential for impacts in these locations will need to be closely monitored as we get into the range of total water level guidance.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A low pressure system and associated occluded front will lift to the north today (the center of the low remains offshore). Showers with this system will move through the terminals through the day. The heaviest showers will remain along the coast, with some of the moisture falling in the interior as virga. VFR ceilings are currently present region-wide. There remains a 40% chance of MVFR post-showers in the south interior/Puget Sound from 15Z to 21Z. Ceilings will improve to VFR this afternoon, and another stronger frontal system will move through Monday with more showers. Surface winds will remain southeasterly at 5 to 10 kt, with some gusts to 20 kt along the waters, and in the Cascades Monday morning. With faster southwest winds just aloft, can't rule out isolated instances of low- level wind-shear as winds come down the Cascades Monday.

KSEA...VFR early this morning, with a 40% chance of MVFR ceilings between 15 and 21Z as the morning round of showers wrap up. Ceilings improve to VFR later in the afternoon with more showers returning later this evening. Winds out of the southeast 5-10 kt.
HPR

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system offshore and occluded front will lift to the north in the coastal waters today. Showers will continue over most waters, with a slight chance of isolated thunderstorms over the coastal waters this afternoon and evening. Southeast winds of 20 to 30 kt will continue in the coastal waters and east Strait of Juan de Fuca, where current small craft advisories will continue into tonight. Another advisory was added for Grays Harbor Bar as seas of 9-12 ft will build today.

The pattern for the remainder of the week remains on track and will be active with several stronger disturbances moving through the waters. The next system late Sunday into Monday will bring widespread southeast winds of 20 to 30 kt with gusts to 35 kt over the previously mentioned waters. The Monday evening through late Tuesday is expected to remain the most impactful, with widespread gale gusts and a greater than 60% chance of wind gusts reaching storm force in the outer coastal waters. Another system passes through Wednesday into Thursday with another round of strong gales in the same waters with a 50% chance of gusts reaching storm force. Additional interior waters will likely see more wind impacts as ensembles have winds turning towards the south and southwest on Thanksgiving day. There is a brief break in winds Friday morning but it will remain breezy for the coastal waters into next weekend with wind gusts still likely breaking 20 kt.
Seas on Monday will build into Tuesday, reaching 18 to 22 ft. They will slightly drop off to 16 to 20 ft Wednesday and Thursday, then drop down to 10 to 12 ft Friday into next weekend.
HPR

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: Wetter systems moving into the region through this week  will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely cross into minor flood stage around midweek onward and continuing to be in flood stage through the weekend. A Hydrologic Outlook has been issued regarding the rainfall and potential river flooding for this timeframe.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active and wet Pacific weather pattern takes hold across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington, bringing multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds through the week. A series of low pressure systems will take aim at the Pacific Northwest, keeping conditions unsettled through Thanksgiving Day and into late week with widespread precipitation and periods of gusty winds. Ensemble guidance shows a low-probability alternative of a stronger, slower-moving low tracking closer to the coast late week, which would increase wind and heavy rain risks.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active and wet Pacific weather pattern takes hold across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington, bringing multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds through the week. A series of low pressure systems will take aim at the Pacific Northwest, keeping conditions unsettled through Thanksgiving Day and into late week with widespread precipitation and periods of gusty winds. Ensemble guidance shows a low-probability alternative of a stronger, slower-moving low tracking closer to the coast late week, which would increase wind and heavy rain risks.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Saturday...An active weather pattern remains the primary focus across the region through the week as a series of low pressure systems and atmospheric rivers keep widespread precipitation in the forecast. The initial system brings the relatively coldest air of the week today, with 850 mb temperatures around -2C holding snow levels mostly between 2500 and 3500 feet, although as low as 2000 ft over the high Cascades. With limited moisture remaining mostly offshore today, snowfall accumulations at Cascade pass levels will stay light, generally under 2 inches, though travelers across the Cascades should still anticipate occasional slick roads during heavier showers.

As we look toward Monday through Wednesday, the weather pattern turns progressively wetter, warmer, and more impactful. A stronger low pressure system will deepen off the northeast Pacific Ocean, coupled with an atmospheric river featuring integrated water vapor transport (IVT) values around 500 kg/(ms) late Monday into Tuesday and 600 kg/(ms) late Wednesday into Thursday. Over a 72-hour period from Monday to Thursday morning, models point to a 50-70% probability for at least 1 inch of rain along the coast, 25-50% across the Cascades, and 10-40% for the inland valleys, with the highest amounts focused north of the Columbia River. With 850 mb temperatures warming during these systems, snow levels will rise to 5000 to 6000 feet, resulting in minimal snow accumulations near pass levels.

In addition to widespread lowland rainfall and mountain snow, coastal communities, beaches, and headlands will experience periods of gusty winds as frontal boundaries sweep onshore. Monday night into Tuesday brings the first round of gusty winds to the coast, where there is a 35-55% chance of peak wind gusts reaching 45 mph or higher, and a 5-10% chance of gusts exceeding 55 mph. Breezy conditions will also extend inland into the lower Columbia River Valley and portions of the Portland metro area at times, though speeds will be notably lower than coastal exposures.

For the calmer sensible weather elements, daytime high temperatures will reach the low to upper 50s along the coast, low to mid 50s for inland valleys, and mid 30s to mid 40s in the Cascades. Overnight lows will remain relatively mild, generally in the upper 30s to mid 40s across the lowlands, though sheltered interior valleys can expect areas of morning valley fog and patchy frost during breaks in precipitation.

Looking toward Thanksgiving Day and the upcoming weekend, model clusters diverge regarding the exact evolution of subsequent Pacific systems. A majority of ensemble members lean toward a ridge of high pressure building over the region starting Friday, which could provide a brief break in precipitation, while alternative cluster solutions maintain unsettled troughing with continued rain. Holiday travelers should monitor later forecasts as details surrounding late-week storm tracks become clearer. ~12

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Monday...As of 11Z Sunday, radar imagery and terminal observations depict light rain and mostly VFR conditions throughout the airspace, with a few terminals under MVFR CIGs. Chances for MVFR CIGs continue until around 19Z Sun as this mornings status deck sits at or below FL045 (chances of MVFR CIGs around 50-70%). Rain showers are expected to scour out or become very sparse at the same time. Thereafter, VFR conditions should persist through the remainder of the TAF period. Around 00-06Z Mon, another band of showers will arrive at the terminals, bringing widespread rain but little to no chance of deteriorated conditions at inland terminals. Coastal terminals could see deteriorated conditions throughout the day with showers passing overhead, with guidance suggesting a 15-25% chance of MVFR conditions at any given hour. Expect south to southeasterly winds around 5-10 kt inland and 10-15 kt with gusts up to 20-25 kt at the coast. KPDX and KTTD will see gusts after 06Z Sun as pressure gradients over the Gorge tighten.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Currently MVFR as rain showers pass overhead. Expect these conditions to continue until around 19Z Sun as guidance suggests a 50-70% of MVFR CIGs through this morning. Expect rain to end and conditions to improve to predominantly VFR thereafter. Widespread rain will return around 06Z Mon, but with no chances of deteriorated conditions. East southeasterly winds continue through the day around 7-10 kt, with gusts up to 18 kt possible after 06Z Mon. ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A frontal system moving through the waters early this morning continues to maintain southerly to southeasterly winds over the waters, bringing small craft wind gusts of 25 kt. Seas are steep and choppy around 9-11 ft at 9-13 seconds, and will gradually build to 12-14 ft through today as a westerly swell moves in. Small Craft Advisories remain in effect through early Monday morning across all waters including the Columbia River Bar.

Active marine conditions continue next week as a series of systems impacts the waters. The next frontal system arrives on Monday, bringing high confidence for another round of gale force wind gusts of 35-40 kt, mainly in the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM. An even stronger system arrives on Tuesday, bringing a 50-70% chance for at least isolated storm force wind gusts up to 48 kt across the outer waters. A Storm Watch for the outer waters and a Gale Watch for the inner waters has been issued from early Monday morning through Tuesday afternoon, including the Columbia River Bar. Seas will also build as a result of the strong winds. There is high confidence (>80% chance) for seas building above 15 ft on Tuesday, and a 30-50% chance for seas above 20 ft for the waters beyond 30 NM offshore. ~12/10

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A Coastal Flood Advisory for tidal overflow remains in effect through 4 AM Tuesday. A Coastal Flood Advisory means that tidal overflow flooding is expected. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property.

Also, a Coastal Flood Watch has been issued as coastal flooding will be possible starting very early Tuesday morning through late Thursday night. The combination of elevated seas, kelvin waves, and a perigean tide (king tide) could result in major flooding. Coastal flood waters up to two foot above ground level along the immediate coast as well as low lying areas near bays, sloughs, and the lower reaches of the coastal rivers will be possible.

Through the upcoming week, a long period swell around 15-17 seconds combined with elevated seas up to 22 ft will result in an elevated sneaker wave threat. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.
